blocks.p: The Mercy Office had built its house on Serenity because nothing on Serenity ever made a sound.

The colony lay deep in the ice of Europa, a honeycomb of warm chambers cut out of an old frozen sea, and the ice took every noise and swallowed it. Footsteps went soft. Voices went soft. Even the machinery that kept the chambers warm gave off no more than a hum that you felt in your teeth rather than heard. Visitors from Abundance spoke of the silence the way people speak of a cold: something that got into you and took a few days to get out.
Sol had always liked it.

They had made the crossing in the night. He had lain down in the stasis pod at the Abundance port with the chill coming up through the cushion and Pell settling into the next pod with a small sigh of contentment, and the last thing he felt was the Halo’s pulse at his temple, faint and steady as a second heartbeat. Then nothing. Then the pulse again, quickening, and warmth in his fingers, and the lid lifting on a blue light that was not Mars. The crossing took a few hours; the stasis made them no time at all. He had made it more times than he could remember, and he had never once dreamed.

Serenity’s port opened onto the Long Gallery, which ran through the ice to the colony’s heart, and the gallery was lit from above by the lanterns: shafts bored straight up to the surface and capped with shielded glass, so that every few hundred paces you passed under a well of light and looked up, and there at the top of it, small and banded and impossibly far, was Jupiter. Sol stopped under the first lantern, as he always did. The planet hung in its circle of glass like an eye. Pell stopped beside him and looked up too, politely, because Sol was looking.

The gravity was the thing one had to remember. On Mars a man weighed a little more than a third of himself; on Europa he weighed almost nothing, and every step wanted to become a leap. The colonists wore weighted boots and walked with a long gliding shuffle, and newcomers could be picked out at once, bobbing along the gallery like corks. Sol had learned the shuffle three centuries ago, and his body remembered it before he did.

The Mercy Office’s holding house stood at the end of a side gallery where the ice had been faced with white stone. There was no sign over the door. There did not need to be. It opened before they reached it, and a woman in white came out to meet them with both hands held out.

“Your Grace. You’re very welcome. I’m Imogen Sallow; I have the house.” She was tall, with a long calm face and grey eyes, and she spoke in the voice all the Mercy Office spoke in, low and even and warm, the voice of a nurse at a bedside at night. “You’ll want to see him first, I expect. He’s resting. He’s been very peaceful.”
“In a moment,” Sol said. “I’d like to see the house.”
“Of course.”

He had seen holding houses on Concord and Titan and in Sion, and had always found them reassuring, and this was the best of them. It was clean the way a thing is clean when people care about it: not merely wiped but tended. The corridors were white and wide and softly lit, and the ice showed through in long panels of glass, blue and deep, with light moving far down inside it. There were no bars. The doors closed without any lock that he could see, and each had a small pane at eye height so the wardens could look in without disturbing anyone. Through one he saw a young woman sitting cross-legged on her bed, combing her hair. Through another, a man asleep with his hand under his cheek. In every room, in a small alcove, a Window glowed.
“They find it calming,” Sallow said. “Most of them pray a great deal while they’re with us.”
“How long are they with you?”

“A few weeks. It depends on the assessment.” She walked with her hands folded in front of her. “We read them when they come in, Your Grace. Not the mind, of course. No one can read a mind. Only the pattern of it, the way it sits in the Halo. And in the infected, the pattern has a fault in it. A place the Halo can’t make sense of.” She considered. “Noise, the technicians call it. Like a wrong note held under the music.”
“And the seizures?”

“Are the fault expressing itself. The mind has grown wrong around the Halo, the way a tree grows wrong around a wire, and every so often it pulls.” She smiled at him. “The wardens have an old name for it. Bad hardware. It isn’t a judgment, you understand. It isn’t the person. It’s the wiring. And wiring can be corrected.”
“At the Hall.”

“At the Hall. They’re reprogrammed and renewed, and they go home.” She said it simply, the way one says that ice is cold. “I’ve been with the Office a hundred and forty years. I’ve never stopped thinking it’s the most merciful work there is.”

Sol believed her. He had always believed it. He had preached it at Concord and at Abundance and in the chapels of Sion: that the Virus was the last sickness left in the new creation, and the Mercy Office its last physician; that the infected were not wicked but wounded; that there was no shame in being carried, and no cruelty in the carrying. He had signed more custody orders than he could count, and he had signed every one of them with a kind of tenderness, as a man signs the papers that send a sick friend to the finest hospital in the world. It had never occurred to him to sign them any other way.

As they passed one door, a woman inside looked up from her bed, saw his robes, and came to the glass. She was young-faced and pale, with a healing bruise on her forehead where she must have fallen. She laid her palm flat on the pane.
“Your Grace,” she said, muffled. “When can I go home?”
“Soon,” Sol said. “Very soon.”
She smiled and took her hand away and went back to her bed. Sallow had stopped beside him. Her face had not changed; it was as calm and kind as before.
“They all ask that,” she said. “It’s a good sign.”
At the end of the corridor she opened the old man’s record for him in the light between their hands.

Hale, Stephen. Born: Earth. Residence: none registered. Received: Abundance, the Bounty Market, on the report of a patron. Custody: Sol Tarren, Bishop of Life. Assessment: pending. Renewal: and then, in the registry’s gentle script, the phrase it used for the denied: Gift not received.
Stephen Hale.

Sol read the name twice. It was an ordinary name. There must have been ten thousand Stephens in the inner colonies and a few hundred Hales. And yet it sat in him oddly, the way a word does that you have not used in years and suddenly find in your mouth, already shaped, before you know you meant to say it. He waited for it to become something. It did not.
“Assessment pending?”

“We’ve been letting him rest,” Sallow said. “He’s very tired. The old ones always are.” She closed the record. “He’s asked for nothing, Your Grace, except that his bag not be taken. I understood that was your instruction.”
“It was.”
“Then it’s been kept.” She touched the door, and it slid aside without a sound. “I’ll be in my office when you’re finished.”

The room was small and white, and one whole wall of it was bare ice, glowing faintly blue with the light of the gallery behind. The Window was in its alcove opposite. The old man was sitting on the edge of the bed with his back to it, facing the ice, his cloth bag on his knees and his spotted hands folded on top of the bag. They had dressed him in the soft white clothes of the house. In the cold blue light his face looked older than it had in the market, the hollows deeper, the skin of his throat finer and looser, and Sol saw that his hands had a small tremor in them that did not stop even when they were still.
He looked up. His eyes were clear.
“You came,” he said.
“I said I would.”
“You did.” The old man smiled. His tongue was still healing, and it thickened his words a little. “You always did what you said. It was one of the more annoying things about you.”
Sol let that pass. He drew the room’s one chair away from the wall and sat. In the low gravity it barely took his weight. “Are you comfortable? Are they treating you well?”
“Very well. They’re very kind. Everyone here is very kind.” The smile turned wry. “I don’t think I’ve ever been treated so kindly in my life.”
“I wanted to tell you myself what will happen. So that you aren’t afraid.”
“That’s good of you.”

So Sol told him. He told it the way he had told it to frightened families on a dozen worlds: the assessment, which was only a reading and did not hurt; the transfer to the Hall, where the fault would be found and corrected; the renewal afterward, which would leave him rested and whole and free of the seizures for good; and then home. He told it well. He had always been able to make the doctrine sound like what it was, a kindness. The old man listened without interrupting, his head a little on one side, with an expression Sol could not quite read. It was the look of someone listening to a child explain, very earnestly, a thing the child has only just learned.
“And then home,” Stephen said, when he had finished.
“Yes.”
“Where’s home, Sol?”
Sol hesitated. “The registry lists no residence. We’ll find you one. There’s room on Concord. There’s room anywhere.”
“That’s kind.” The old man looked down at his hands. “I won’t be renewed.”
“I know you’ve refused it before. I understand that there may have been reasons...”
“I haven’t refused it. I’ve just told you a fact.” He said it gently, almost apologetically. “I won’t be renewed.”
“It isn’t a punishment. It’s part of the cure. Without it...”

He stopped. He had been about to say without it you’ll go on as you are, and he heard, before he said it, where the sentence went after that. The old man would go on as he was. He would go on getting older, his hands shaking a little more each season, his skin loosening, his hair thinning, until one day he would simply stop. Sol had known that, in the way one knows a fact in a book. He had never once sat in a chair across from it.
“You can’t know that,” he said.
“I can, actually. It’s one of the very few things I know for certain these days.” Stephen raised his eyes. “Don’t trouble yourself over it. Truly. It’s not the worst thing.”

Sol did not know what to say to that, so he said nothing. The silence of Serenity came into the room and sat with them. Somewhere deep in the ice wall there was a long, low tick, the sound the ice made as it settled, like a great house shifting in its sleep.
“You called me by my name,” Sol said at last. “In the market.”
“I did.”
“Why?”
“Because it’s your name.” The old man seemed to consider how to go on, and then decided to go on simply. “We knew each other once.”

Sol had expected it, and still it moved through him strangely, like the name on the record. He set it aside, as he had set the name aside, and leaned forward with his elbows on his knees, the way he leaned toward the bereaved.
“I don’t think so,” he said gently.
“No. You wouldn’t.”

“It’s not uncommon, you know. After a seizure the mind reaches for something to hold on to. A face, a name. It builds a bridge out of whatever is nearest. You saw a bishop. Perhaps someone had told you my name once, years ago, and your mind...”
“Built a bridge,” Stephen said. “That’s well put. You always did put things well.”
“I have worn this face since the Judgment. I’ve held the same office, kept the same friends. I would remember.”
“Would you?”

It was asked without any edge at all. It was asked the way one asks a real question, wanting to know. The ice ticked again in the wall. Sol found that he had an answer ready, and that the answer was yes, and that it was taking him a moment longer than it should have to say it.
“Yes,” he said.
The old man nodded slowly, like a man conceding a point in a game he had not much minded losing. “Then it’s a delusion.”
“I think it is. And I think it’s a symptom, and that it can be healed, and that you’ll be glad of it afterward.” Sol said it kindly, because he meant it kindly. “You’ll be at peace.”
“You’re kind, Sol. You were always kind. People forget that about you.”

The pressure had come back behind Sol’s left eye while they talked, quietly, a thumb pressed from inside. He found that he had raised two fingers to his brow without deciding to. He lowered them. The old man was watching him with an expression that was not wry at all.
“You should have that looked at,” Stephen said.
“It’s the light.”
Stephen glanced at the soft white ceiling, and then at the blue ice, and then back at Sol, and said nothing.
“You have your back to the Window,” Sol said, to say something else.
“Yes.”
“Wouldn’t you rather face it? The wardens say it helps.”
“I’d rather look at the ice.” The old man turned his head toward it. The blue light lay along his cheek. “It’s honest. It’s exactly what it looks like, all the way down.”

Sol’s eyes went to the bag on his knees. It was a plain thing of undyed cloth, worn soft, with a drawstring, and it sat on the old man’s lap with an odd heaviness, as if it held more than it should. Stephen’s hands had not moved from it once.
“What do you keep in there?”
“Old things,” Stephen said, and his hands stayed where they were.
Sol stood. “If you need anything, ask the wardens. They’ll send for me.”
“You’ll come back.”
“If you’d like.”

“I would. Not today, I think. Today you’ve got your failures.” When Sol looked at him, he smiled. “Everyone knows why the bishop is in the colonies, Sol. Even the denied hear things.” He was quiet a moment. “Come back when you’re tired of tidy answers.”

Sol stood very still. It was only a phrase. People said it. Aurelian had said it two nights before, on the other side of the solar system, through the relay of Sion, and it meant nothing that a sick old man under the ice of Europa had said it too. He nodded, and touched the door, and it opened.
“Sol.”
He turned.
“It’s good to see you,” Stephen said. He said it plainly, warmly, as one says it to a friend at the end of a long absence, and then he turned back to the ice.
Sallow’s office was a small white room with a single panel of ice for a wall and a desk with nothing on it. She rose when he came in.
“I’m here about the ascension failures as well,” Sol said. “There have been five on Serenity. I’d like to know whether any of them passed through this house. Families, witnesses, anyone.”
“I’ll check, Your Grace, but I’d be surprised.” She opened the ledger between them, and the house’s records rose into the light in long, orderly rows. “We keep everything. You’re welcome to it.”

Each row held a name and a face, an origin, a date of intake. There was a column for the witness who had made the report: a neighbor, a coworker, her husband, his daughter, a patron. There was a column for the assessment, and in nearly every row it read noise confirmed. And there was a final column, and in every row the final column read the same.
Transferred to Mercy Hall for reprogramming.

Forty-one rows this year. Sol let the ledger run back. Last year: thirty-eight, and every one of them transferred. The year before. Ten years before. The column ran down through the decades in a single unbroken line of gentle script, and it was some time before he understood what was bothering him about it, and when he understood, it was not a thing in the ledger. It was a thing that was not in it.
There was no column for afterward. No discharged. No returned. No home.
“None of your five are here, Your Grace,” Sallow said. “I’m sorry.”
“Where are the discharges recorded?”

“At the Hall.” She did not seem surprised by the question. “Once they’re transferred, they’re in Mercy, and the Hall keeps its own books. The families are told their loved ones are in Mercy. And then one day they’re home.”
“Have you ever seen one come home?”
He asked it lightly. She smiled at him with perfect patience.
“We’re a holding house, Your Grace. We wouldn’t.”

He told himself it was a reasonable answer. He stood looking at the long column of names and tried to think of a single person, in all those years, who had come to him afterward and said I was in Mercy, and now I am well, and he thought he could. There had been a woman on Concord once, a weaver, he thought, who had waited at the cathedral door after a service to take his hand. He could see the door quite clearly. He could not see her face.

And then the answer came to him, and it was so simple that he almost smiled. Of course they never thanked him. They were renewed. Whatever they had suffered, the Virus and the seizures and the fear, had been gently taken from them, as every grief was taken. They went home without the memory of having been ill. They could not thank anyone for a mercy they did not know they had received. That was the whole beauty of it.
He was still standing there when Pell came in, a little out of breath from hurrying in boots that were not heavy enough.

“Your Grace. Forgive me. The infirmary in the lower workings has asked for you. There’s been a fall of ice in the north shafts, and one of the drill crew is badly hurt. They don’t expect him to last the afternoon.” Pell lowered his voice. “The chaplain asks whether you would preside. Given the failures, he says. He would rather it were you.”
“I’ll come now,” Sol said.

He followed Pell out into the white corridor. Behind him, in the warden’s quiet office, the ledger still hung open in the light above the empty desk, forty-one names long this year, every line ending in the same place.
